# Color pop

- Route: `/tools/color-pop`
- Kind: `tool`
- Category: `photo`
- Slug: `color-pop`

## Summary

Keep the reds, or the blues, or any one of six color families, and turn everything else gray with a single built-in look you can tune afterwards. (Photo editing)

## Details

This page opens Aperture, the Media Manipulator photo editor, with the Color (HSL) panel in front and the look called Color pop: red already applied. A look adds its adjustments to the stack as a group, and this one is a single Color (HSL) layer whose six ranges are set so that Reds get Saturation +10 and Yellows, Greens, Cyans, Blues and Magentas each get Saturation -100. The effect is the classic selective color photo: one hue family survives, everything else collapses to gray. Five sibling looks keep yellow, green, cyan, blue or magenta instead, and the Gray except this chips in the panel do the same thing for any range in one click, including a custom range you picked with the eyedropper.
### What it does
- Applies Color pop: red on open, one Color (HSL) layer with Reds Saturation +10 and the other five ranges at Saturation -100, and lists Color pop: yellow, green, cyan, blue and magenta in the Looks panel for the other families.
- The Gray except this chip next to any range, including a custom eyedropper range, sets every other range to -100 saturation in one click, so a particular orange or purple can be the kept color.
- Each kept range has Width (10 to 120 degrees) and Feather (0 to 90) sliders that decide how much of the neighbouring hues survive, which is how you keep orange with the reds or exclude it.
- The neutral fade leaves grays alone, the kept range can be nudged with its own Hue and Lightness sliders, and the whole look can be masked, lowered in opacity or removed with one undo.
- The export renders the original at full resolution with the same six-range formula and names the file (retouched).
### How to use it
1. Drop the photo: The editor opens full screen on the Color (HSL) panel with Color pop: red applied as a group of one layer.
2. Choose the color to keep: Switch to Color pop: blue, green, yellow, cyan or magenta in Looks, or press Gray except this on any range, including one you picked from the photo.
3. Widen or narrow the kept range: Raise Width to include neighbouring hues, lower it to isolate one; use the mask overlay or the histogram to check what survived.
4. Export: JPG, PNG, WebP, AVIF or TIFF at the quality you choose, rendered by the server from the original pixels.
### Supported formats
- Input: JPG, PNG, WebP, GIF, HEIC, HEIF, AVIF, TIFF, BMP
- Output: JPG, PNG, WebP, AVIF, TIFF
- The look is one layer of per-pixel HSL math; export time is set by the encoder and the pixel count, a few seconds for a 12 megapixel JPG.
- A look applied through the page is a layer group you can rename, mask or delete like any other layer.
### Technical details
- Saturation per pixel is s multiplied by the product over ranges of 1 + weight x Saturation/100. Inside a range at -100 the factor is 1 - weight, so a pixel fully inside Blues gets factor 0 and becomes gray; inside the kept Reds range at +10 the factor is 1.1, a ten percent lift. Hue and lightness are never changed by the look.
- Range weights come from the circular distance to the range center with the default Width 30 and Feather 30: full at 15 degrees or less, zero at 45 or more, linear between. A pixel exactly between two ranges, such as orange at hue 30, carries weight 0.5 in both, so with Reds kept it multiplies saturation by 1.05 x 0.5 = 0.525.
- Between two desaturated ranges the product of the two factors matters: at hue 210, halfway between Cyans and Blues, each weight is 0.5 and the saturation factor is 0.5 x 0.5 = 0.25, not 0, so a sky there keeps a quarter of its color. Raising Width on both ranges to 60 makes their cores meet at 210 and the factor falls to 0.
- Every range weight is scaled by min(1, s / 0.1), so a pixel with HSL saturation below 0.1 gets a proportionally smaller lift in the kept range; it is already nearly gray and the -100 ranges have little to remove.
- The look is stored as an ordinary layer group in the project: Looks are additive, Undo removes the whole group, and your own variants can be saved as a preset in this browser or exported as JSON.
- Your screen shows a WebGL2 render from a 1920 px copy; the exported file is produced on our server from the original with the same range math, within the documented tolerance for color operations of a mean error of at most 1 and a maximum of 4 levels in 8 bits.
### When not to use it
Selective color keeps a hue wherever it occurs, so when two objects share a color and only one should stay colored you need a Brush or Radial mask on the look, or Select subject, rather than a wider or narrower range. It is not the way to get a clean monochrome, because a kept range at +10 and five ranges at -100 still leave quarter-strength color at the seams; use the black and white page for that. If what you want is a stronger or softer version of every color, the saturation page does it in one slider, and if the goal is to change the kept color rather than keep it, go to the object color page.
### Use cases
- Street photography accents: Keep the reds for a coat, a bus or a sign in a monochrome street scene; the Reds range catches them all at once.
- Product on gray: Keep the brand color of a product and let the set, the hands and the props go gray around it.
- Wedding and event details: Keep the flowers or the dress color against a gray room; a mask on the look restricts it to the table if the carpet shares the hue.
- Doors, boats and cars: Color pop: blue or Color pop: yellow for a single painted object; widen the kept range if the paint drifts toward cyan or orange in the shade.
### FAQ
Q: Which colors can I keep?
A: Any of the six named ranges through the Color pop looks, Reds, Yellows, Greens, Cyans, Blues and Magentas, and any other hue by clicking it in the photo with the eyedropper and pressing Gray except this on the new custom range.
Q: Why is my sky still slightly blue after Color pop: red?
A: A sky at hue 210 sits halfway between Cyans and Blues, so each range gives it weight 0.5 and the two -100 factors multiply to 0.25, leaving a quarter of the saturation. Raise Width on both ranges to 60 so their cores overlap at 210 and the factor drops to zero.
Q: Why do faces keep some color with the reds kept?
A: Skin sits around hue 20, inside the Reds range, so the look keeps it by design. A pixel at (217, 158, 128) loses only about 11 percent of its saturation. Narrow the Reds Width, or add a Brush mask with Subtract over the face, if you want skin gray.
Q: Can I keep two colors at once?
A: Yes. The look is a normal Color (HSL) layer, so after it is applied set a second range, for example Yellows, back from -100 to 0, or press Gray except this on a custom range and then restore any named range you also want.
Q: Is the effect reversible after I export?
A: The export is a new file named with (retouched) and your original is never modified. Inside the project the look is a layer group: Undo removes it, and the layer can be hidden or deleted at any time.
Q: What does the +10 on the kept range do?
A: It multiplies the saturation of pixels fully inside the kept range by 1.1 so the surviving color reads a little stronger against the gray around it. Set it back to 0 if you want the kept color exactly as shot.

## Routing

When to send a visitor here: Use when someone wants selective colour: keep the reds (or yellows, greens, cyans, blues, magentas, or an eyedropper colour) and turn everything else grey. Typical asks: "black and white except the red dress".
When to send them elsewhere: For a clean full monochrome use Black & white photo (black-and-white-photo). For stronger or weaker colours overall use Image saturation (image-saturation). To change the kept colour rather than keep it use Change object color (change-image-color).
Related tools: black-and-white-photo (full monochrome conversion); image-saturation (overall colour strength); change-image-color (recolour instead of isolate); select-by-color (precise colour masks)
